title: Young people are useful to society as heretics, not as good citizens
dek: College trains young people to be good citizens, but what society actually needs is for them to question what everyone takes for granted; in the AI era every student can build their own projects, they just need permission.
why: Medium information density, but Amjad's path from chess to training models to building new Replit products is very concrete, useful for judging whether young people should start companies now.
who: Young people agonizing over whether to go to college or start a company now, plus founders, investors and early-stage backers who want to understand how AI changes organizational forms.
skip: The sci-fi novel recap at the start, 0:00-2:04, can be skipped; go straight to the argument from 4:07.

points.h: Young people are useful as heretics
points.body: Amjad uses the sci-fi novel The City and the Stars as an analogy: in that city governed by an AGI, everyone is repeatedly reborn from compressed memories, until the machine breaks down and a genuinely new person is born, who immediately starts asking ‘what's outside the walls’. Amjad says the use of young people is to ask exactly this kind of question, to be heretics. But today's universities do the opposite — they tell you ‘we've already figured everything out, just learn our way’, and train you into a good citizen: marry, have kids, buy a house, buy a car. The problem is that world no longer exists; you can perform brilliantly in college and still end up unemployed with a pile of debt.

points.h: Silicon Valley is itself a monoculture
points.body: Amjad says every society has blind spots, and Silicon Valley has plenty — it's a monoculture with a fixed way of thinking, so many ideas simply won't grow out of Silicon Valley. Even the most radical culture is, at bottom, a monoculture. So you need young people to experiment, to attempt what's considered impossible, and occasionally someone breaks through: impossible yesterday, suddenly possible today because the technology changed. What college should do is gather clear-minded, first-principles thinkers and encourage them to question the things that are deeply believed.

points.h: Raising at 18 is an overused option
points.body: Gagan says young people today face a wildly unfair binary: either go to a four-year college and be managed by attendance, homework, exams and grades, or tomorrow someone hands you $50,000 to start a company. He thinks the investor path should be used far less, and only a tiny number of teenagers should raise money. Most people at 17 or 18 know they want to enter the business world, but having two years to explore and learn without pressure is precious. He argues for a middle ground: two years to explore freely, with Silicon Valley actively sending information and resources your way, and more support if you have a good idea.

points.h: Starting too early is premature optimization
points.body: Amjad borrows a programming phrase, ‘premature optimization is the root of all evil’: a lot of founding is premature optimization. He sees many kids now inside a circle where friends are raising big rounds, some became unicorns, so the motivation becomes a negative one like envy, and then they pre-commit to an idea they aren't even interested in, optimizing early for a path they haven't reached yet. He says the real question is what your curiosity is driving you toward; once you find the idea you'd be willing to spend ten years, a lifetime on, it has enormous gravity and you can't dodge it — he himself actively didn't want to start a company, but the thing blew up into one on its own. He also says VCs now go to Stanford and give students a million dollars with no idea yet, so there's already a cap table before you've done anything, which is a bit like the music industry signing young artists.

points.h: From chess all the way to training models
points.body: Amjad says he's always oscillated between ‘wanting to build things’ and ‘wanting to read and explore widely’, the two feeding each other in a recursive process. He gives his recent obsession with chess as an example: he started playing very late, doesn't know why he was interested, then started writing programs to solve chess and train models, and found that LLMs are terrible at chess and hallucinate moves that don't exist. To figure it out, he'd never trained a model, yet spent a lot of time studying how to train one. He realized from this that AI can now do machine learning itself, just as in 2024 Replit's agent suddenly learned to write code and afterward coding changed completely — machine learning may be at that same moment, which he calls vibe research or auto research. He's now building products at Replit to let anyone become a machine learning researcher, or let a boss with data fine-tune a model to solve a specific problem.

Amjad thinks the shape of companies will change. Silicon Valley has tried many experiments to remake companies — Holacracy, Medium tried it, GitHub tried a no-manager system, all failed spectacularly, but he thinks that was a technology problem: now you can have agents act as the glue in an organization, turn bureaucratic processes into invisible things machines do in the background, while people get real autonomy to work on what interests them most, and AI can even judge your impact. He says he's already changed how management works at Replit, calls it a ‘self-driving company’, and eventually the company will run itself. He admits he doesn't have a fully formed idea, but he's certain everything will change, and much faster than you think; if you don't natively understand this stuff, the transition will be hard.

points.h: Trust makes money arrive six weeks faster
points.body: Gagan says he volunteers in local politics in his spare time, and the biggest takeaway is understanding how valuable trust is. He gives a concrete comparison: in a nonprofit, after a donor verbally commits $50,000 to you, the probability that the money actually lands in your account is only about 20% to 50%; in Silicon Valley, that probability is about 75% to 100%. The difference is that if you're confident the money is coming, you can push forward with confidence, and by the time the check actually arrives you've already advanced six weeks, which makes the check even more valuable. Conversely, without trust you change your approach out of fear the donor will be unhappy, drift from your mission, and are left with only anxiety and stress. He thinks this can be transplanted into schools: trust students to do what they want to do.

points.h: No grades means no fulcrum to push against
points.body: Asked how to handle disruptive students — like Zuckerberg, who nearly got expelled for FaceMash — Gagan says there obviously have to be red lines, things like sexual harassment and publicly humiliating others need rules, and you need to build trust and a positive-sum atmosphere. But he says one core principle of the academy sidesteps the problem entirely: no grades, no exams, so the resistance students have to push against is already much smaller. So if you want to build FaceMash, go build it, and he's willing to defend that right even if he personally finds the idea weird and doesn't like it. He thinks that as long as you create an environment of trust and don't let students develop an anti-authority mindset, you can unlock a huge amount of creativity and opportunity. Amjad adds that this drive to test boundaries can be channeled in healthy directions: kids who learn to code and hack on Roblox, rather than being sent to prison, could be given sandboxes, have their talent discovered, and be steered into cybersecurity jobs or even government.

terms.def: In programming, optimizing code before you know what matters; Amjad uses it as a metaphor for starting a company too early.
An organizational form that removes management hierarchy and runs on self-governing roles; Medium and GitHub tried it and failed.
Amjad's phrase: agents take on bureaucratic processes and the company eventually runs itself.
Amjad's name for AI doing machine learning research itself, by analogy with vibe coding.
The Aristotelian ethical view: act in a way you wouldn't be ashamed of whether or not anyone is watching.
